blocks.passage:
Financing trade in emerging markets requires a different mindset. Many of the standard tools — cheap local bank credit, simple export insurance, frictionless FX — are partly available or not available at all. What works instead is creativity plus local knowledge.

In practice, this often means a blend: a local bank for daily operations, a multilateral institution (like the IFC or EBRD) for larger tranches, and a private credit fund for the gaps. Each partner has its own rules, its own speed, and its own appetite for risk.

I'd argue that the single biggest factor is not the product — it's the relationships. A trusted local partner, a banker who knows your business, and a line that has been tested once before a crisis: those three things open more doors than any clever structure.

options: The same tools as developed markets
A different mindset — creativity plus local knowledge
items.why: "requires a different mindset… creativity plus local knowledge."

items.q: What is often partly available or unavailable in emerging markets?
options: Standard tools like cheap local credit and frictionless FX
items.why: "Many of the standard tools… are partly available or not available at all."

items.q: What does the 'blend' typically include?
options: A local bank, a multilateral institution, and a private credit fund
items.why: "a local bank for daily operations, a multilateral institution… and a private credit fund for the gaps."

items.q: What does the author argue is the single biggest factor?
items.why: "the single biggest factor is not the product — it's the relationships."

items.q: Why is 'a line that has been tested once before a crisis' valuable?
options: You know it will actually work when you need it most
It is faster to set up
items.why: Inferência: uma linha já testada dá confiança de que funcionará na hora da crise.

audio.text:
You're setting up a new sugar operation in Angola, and you asked how to fund it. Forget the textbook — the standard tools we'd use in Europe are only half available here. This needs a blend and a lot of local knowledge.

Here's the stack I'd build. For daily operations — paying farmers, local costs — use a local bank. They're not cheap, but they understand the market and they move fast on the ground.

For the big tranche, the capital expenditure, go to a multilateral like the IFC. They lend larger amounts at better rates for exactly this kind of development, and their involvement actually reassures other lenders.

Then, for the gaps the other two won't cover, a private credit fund. More expensive, but flexible, and they'll take a risk the banks won't.

But honestly? The structure is the easy part. What really matters is the relationships. Find a trusted local partner on the ground, get a banker who genuinely knows your business, and test a small line before you need a big one. In an emerging market, a tested relationship opens more doors than any clever structure on paper.

items.q: Why does James say to 'forget the textbook'?
options: The standard tools are only half available in Angola
items.why: "the standard tools we'd use in Europe are only half available here."

items.q: What does James suggest using for daily operations?
options: A local bank that understands the market and moves fast
items.why: "For daily operations… use a local bank. They… understand the market and they move fast on the ground."

items.q: Why go to a multilateral like the IFC for the big tranche?
options: They lend larger amounts at better rates and reassure other lenders
They are the cheapest for daily costs
items.why: "They lend larger amounts at better rates… and their involvement actually reassures other lenders."

items.q: What is the role of the private credit fund?
options: Covering the gaps the other two won't, taking risks banks won't
items.why: "for the gaps the other two won't cover, a private credit fund… they'll take a risk the banks won't."

items.q: What does James say really matters most?
options: The relationships — a trusted local partner and a tested line
items.why: "What really matters is the relationships… a tested relationship opens more doors than any clever structure."

items.q: An **emerging market** is…
options: a developing economy with growing but less mature financial systems
items.why: Emerging market = mercado emergente.

items.q: A **multilateral institution** (like the IFC) is…
options: an international body backed by several governments that funds development
items.why: Multilateral institution = instituição multilateral.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "We fund the big part with one large **___**."
items.why: Tranche = tranche, fatia de financiamento.

items.q: A fund's **appetite** for risk means…
options: how much risk it is willing to take
items.why: Appetite = apetite (por risco).

items.q: Choose the correct term: "We use a **___** of local bank, multilateral and private fund."
items.why: Blend = mescla, combinação.

items.q: "Let's **build a stack** of funding sources." To build a stack means to…
items.why: Build a stack = montar camadas/combinação de fontes.

items.q: "The IFC's involvement **reassures** other lenders." To reassure means to…
items.why: Reassure = dar confiança, tranquilizar.

items.q: "Test a small line before you **scale up**." To scale up means to…
items.why: Scale up = ampliar.

items.q: "A tested relationship **opens doors**." To open doors means to…
items.why: Open doors = abrir portas/oportunidades.

items.q: "On the ground, they **know the ropes**." To know the ropes means to…
options: be experienced and know how things work
items.why: Know the ropes = ter experiência, saber como funciona.
